title: Rear suspension: meet the team keeping your Mustang planted
introduction:
I think of the rear suspension as a team with very different jobs. The springs hold the car up and soak up movement; the shocks keep the aftermath from becoming a damn pogo-stick convention. Arms and links guide the wheels, while the hubs and bearings let them turn. Once those jobs click, the names stop sounding like a shopping list from another planet.

Let’s follow the parts from the chassis to the wheel and see who does what. This is a parts-and-purpose tour; use the matching service procedure when you’re ready to inspect, adjust or replace something.

edits.text: How the rear suspension fits together
I sort this component list by job: support the load, calm the bouncing, guide the wheels, and let the wheel assemblies turn. Much easier than memorizing a pile of part names.
Coil springs — support vehicle load and compress and expand as the wheels move over bumps.
edits.why: The spring stores and releases energy. Its partner, the shock absorber, keeps that energy from turning into an endless encore.

edits.text: Lower arm and bushing assemblies — guide the wheel knuckles as the suspension travels.
edits.why: The arms’ mounting points and bushings help guide that movement. I match the full component name when looking up its service procedure.

edits.text: Shock absorbers — resist suspension motion and control how quickly bouncing settles.
edits.why: The spring supports the load; the shock controls movement. Same team, different job descriptions.

edits.text: Stabilizer bar and links — work together to resist suspension lean/sway and side-to-side body roll.
edits.why: The links connect the bar to the suspension, allowing it to work alongside the springs and shock absorbers.

edits.text: Toe links — help control the direction the rear wheels point when viewed from above.
edits.why: Toe is the direction a wheel points when viewed from above. I picture looking down at my own feet to remember the term.

edits.text: Upper arms — help locate the wheel knuckles relative to the chassis while allowing suspension travel.
edits.why: Their role is to guide the wheel’s movement.

edits.text: Lower arm vertical links — a separate named component from the lower arm and bushing assemblies.
edits.why: I keep those names separate when matching a part to its service procedure; similar names are not interchangeable parts.

edits.text: Wheel bearing and wheel hub assemblies — carry the mounted wheels and allow the hubs to rotate while supporting load.
edits.why: The hub supports the wheel and its studs; the bearing allows the hub to turn.

edits.text: Wheel knuckles — carry the wheel hubs and connect them to the suspension’s locating links.
edits.why: The knuckle provides the structural connection between the rotating wheel assembly and the parts that guide suspension travel.

edits.text: Wheel studs — threaded fasteners used with wheel nuts to secure the wheels to the hubs.
edits.why: The studs and wheel nuts work together to fasten the wheel to the hub.

edits.text: I trace the wheel-guiding arrangement through the 2 parallel arms (1 upper and 1 lower). Each arm mounts to the chassis and attaches to the wheel knuckle, guiding its movement while allowing the rear wheels to respond independently to road imperfections. The shock absorber mounts to the lower arm and works with the spring to control vertical movement: the spring supports load and stores energy as it compresses, while the shock absorber resists motion and helps it settle. The stabilizer bar and links control suspension lean/sway. I keep those jobs separate when reading the layout: vertical movement and body roll involve connected parts with different roles.
edits.why: Independent wheel response lets the rear wheels accommodate different road imperfections. The stabilizer bar still links the sides to resist body roll: independent does not mean each side has quit the team.
